chapters.title: Your Brain Explained
chapters.intro: Before anything else, meet the organ running the show. The book opens by asking what the brain actually is: a computer, a thinking machine, a fatty pink organ, and a vast collection of neurons all at once, and 'more complex than anything in the known universe' (p. 5). This chapter covers what the brain does, how neurons and nerves carry its signals, how scientists map its wiring, and why the spinal cord is really part of the brain.
objectives: Describe the brain's core jobs in everyday terms
Explain what neurons are and how signals travel
Understand what TrackVis brain maps show
Explain the gray matter / white matter split and the spinal cord's role

topics.title: What the brain is and what it does

intro.what: The brain is the body's coordination and interpretation centre: a fatty pink organ made of roughly 86 billion nerve cells.
intro.why: Everything you think, remember, feel and do runs through it, so understanding it is the foundation for the whole book.
intro.where: It sits inside the skull, connected to the rest of the body through the spinal cord and nerve network.
intro.problem: It interprets the outside world and makes sense of it, while consuming energy effortlessly, storing memories, processing thoughts and letting you react to danger (p. 5).

topics.explanation: The book compares the brain to several things at once. It is like a computer because it registers memories that can be quickly recalled and determines movements. It is like a vast collection of neurons because, in a sense, its main function is interpreting the outside world and making sense of it (p. 6). Information from the body moves up the spinal cord to the brain stem, then on to the cerebral cortex, which controls thoughts and memories. Neurons work like electrical circuits: signals in a logical sequence cause neurons to bond with other neurons, and this chain reaction happens incredibly fast, yet it might help you compose a symphony or recall entire passages of a book (p. 5). Neurologist Dr Robert Melillo, founder of the Brain Balance centers, is cited in the book as an expert on how the brain's structure supports these functions (pp. 6-8).
topics.mechanism: Sensory information enters, travels along nerves to the spinal cord, ascends to the brain stem, and reaches the cortex where it is interpreted and stored. Motor plans travel the reverse route. Each perception or action is the firing of circuits of linked neurons, sequenced so that the right cells activate in the right order.
components: Cerebral cortex: outer sheet handling thoughts, memories and interpretation
Brain stem: relay hub between body and cortex
Spinal cord: the information cable between brain and body
Neurons: the signalling cells, working like electrical circuits

examples.title: Recalling a book passage
examples.text: You quote a paragraph you read years ago. The chain of neurons that stored it re-fires in sequence, letting you recall entire passages almost instantly.
examples.mechanism: A stored neural circuit re-activates in the same logical sequence it was written in.

examples.title: Reacting to danger
examples.text: A ball flies at your face and you flinch before you consciously decide to. The brain's fast interpretation path, via brain stem and spinal cord circuits, drives the reaction.
examples.mechanism: Sensory signal, rapid subcortical processing, motor output.

examples.title: Making sense of a noisy room
examples.text: At a party you can still follow one conversation. The cortex weighs incoming sound against context and attention to interpret which stream matters.
examples.mechanism: Cortical interpretation prioritises some inputs over others.

connections: Feeds directly into Neurons explained (c01t2) and the nervous-system hierarchy (c03).
The 'interpretation' idea reappears in How the Brain Sees (c07) and optical illusions (c18), where interpretation goes wrong in instructive ways.
takeaways: The brain simultaneously resembles a computer, a thinking machine and a fatty pink organ (p. 5).
Its central job is interpreting the outside world and making sense of it (p. 6).
Signals travel body → spinal cord → brain stem → cerebral cortex.
Neurons bond in chains and fire in fast logical sequences.
A single circuit can support everything from symphonies to memory recall.

topics.title: Neurons explained and brain maps

intro.what: A tour of the neuron, the brain's basic signalling cell, plus TrackVis, a free program neurologists use to map the brain's fibre connections.
intro.why: Neurons are the units everything else in the book is built from; brain maps show how those units are wired together.
intro.where: Neurons live throughout the brain and nervous system; TrackVis maps are generated from MRI scans of whole brains.
intro.problem: How does a feeling arising in one part of the brain reach another part? Through the fibre pathways TrackVis makes visible.

topics.explanation: The book's standfirst says it plainly: 'Neurons are like electrical circuits' (p. 7). A neuron receives signals, and when the combined input crosses its threshold it fires an electrical impulse down its fibre to the next cell. Repeated signalling strengthens the connection, which is the basis of both learning (c16) and muscle memory (c02). TrackVis is a free program used by neurologists to see a map of the brain that shows the fibre connections. On every brain, these neural pathways help connect one part of the brain to another so that a feeling you experience in one part of the brain can be transmitted to another part that must act on it (p. 7). Seeing the wiring means clinicians can check whether major highways between regions are intact after injury or disease.
topics.mechanism: An electrical signal travels down a neuron's axon; at its tip chemical messengers cross a tiny gap to the next neuron, continuing the chain. Diffusion MRI reconstruction (the maths behind TrackVis) infers the direction of water movement along axon bundles, drawing the brain's wiring diagram from scanning data.
components: Neuron: signalling cell with receiving branches and a transmitting fibre
Synapse: the gap where signals pass chemically between neurons
Neural pathway: a bundle of connected neurons linking brain regions
TrackVis: free software that renders fibre-connection maps from MRI

examples.title: A thought moving across the brain
examples.text: You hear a song and suddenly feel sad: the auditory region's activity travels along mapped pathways to emotion regions, exactly the cross-brain transmission TrackVis visualises.
examples.mechanism: Signals propagate along fibre pathways linking distant regions.

examples.title: Neurologists checking wiring after injury
examples.text: After a head injury a clinician can use a fibre map to see whether connections between regions look disrupted, guiding diagnosis and rehab.
examples.mechanism: MRI diffusion data rendered by TrackVis shows tract integrity.

connections: Neuron firing is the engine of the action potential simulator (Lab).

topics.title: Nerves, the spinal cord and gray vs white matter

intro.what: Nerves are the body's transmission cables; the spinal cord is structurally part of the brain, with its gray and white matter arranged inside-out compared to the brain.
intro.why: Explains how signals physically travel between brain and toes, and a classic exam-style fact about tissue arrangement.
intro.where: Nerves run through the whole body; the spinal cord runs inside the backbone from the brain stem downward.
intro.problem: How does a signal get from your toenail up to your brain? Nerves carry it the whole way.

topics.explanation: 'Nerves are the transmission cables that carry brain waves in the human body,' says Sol Diamond, an assistant professor at the Thayer School of Engineering at Dartmouth (p. 8). Nerves communicate these signals from one point to another, whether from your toenail up to your brain or from the side of your head. Scientists have known for the past 100 years or so that the spinal cord is actually part of the brain (p. 8). The difference is arrangement: the brain has gray matter on the outside, protected by the skull, with white matter protected on the inside. The spinal cord is reversed, with gray matter inside and white matter outside. Gray matter is dense with neuron cell bodies doing the processing; white matter is the insulated cabling that carries signals long distances.
topics.mechanism: A signal generated at a fingertip enters a peripheral nerve, ascends the spinal cord's white-matter tracts, relays through the brain stem and reaches the cortex. Motor commands descend the same cables in the opposite direction.
components: Nerves: transmission cables carrying signals between body and brain
Gray matter: neuron cell bodies, the processing layer
White matter: insulated fibre tracts, the cabling layer
Spinal cord: part of the brain, gray inside / white outside

examples.title: Toenail to brain
examples.text: You stub your toe: the signal runs up a nerve, through the spinal cord, to the brain, where it becomes pain. Diamond's toenail example is literally this route (p. 8).
examples.mechanism: Long peripheral nerves plus spinal tracts carry the signal the full distance.

examples.title: Inside-out wiring
examples.text: Think of the spinal cord as the brain's cable rolled up backwards: processing core in the middle, cabling wrapped around the outside.
examples.mechanism: Reversed gray/white arrangement accommodates tracts running up and down.

connections: Sets up the reflex arc (c03t3): fastest signals never wait for the cortex.

chapters.title: What Is Muscle Memory?
chapters.intro: How do practiced movements become automatic? The book's answer: neural shortcuts in your brain make practiced activities feel familiar (p. 9), built by repetition of movements that creates a strong connection between the muscles and brain (p. 10).
objectives: Explain how walking goes from conscious effort to automatic
Describe the muscle anatomy terms on p. 10 (perimysium, fasciculus)
Connect repetition to strengthened neural pathways

topics.title: Neural shortcuts: from wobbly steps to automatic walking

intro.what: Muscle memory is the ability to perform practiced movements with little conscious thought, thanks to neural shortcuts formed by repetition.
intro.why: It explains why you can walk, type, or ride a bike without analysing every step.
intro.where: The loop runs between muscles, spinal cord and the brain's motor areas.
intro.problem: Newborns cannot walk; adults walk without thinking. Repetition bridges that gap.

topics.explanation: When you move from one side of the room to the other, how much do you analyse the action? For most people the series of muscle movements that get them around daily is automatic (p. 9). But babies are born with brains that must learn to coordinate muscles in order to stand and balance. Through trial and error, and repeated practice of walking, the neural pathways are fully formed. From that point onwards, walking becomes a natural motion requiring little conscious thought (p. 9). The repetition of movements creates a strong connection between the muscles and brain (p. 10). Each practice session literally tunes the circuit: the more often a movement sequence fires, the easier and more reliable that firing becomes, which is why the book calls it a neural shortcut. The muscle side has its own hierarchy of parts: perimysium, the connective tissue sheath that surrounds fibre bundles and protects them from forceful contractions, and the fasciculus, bundles of nerve-related fibres running within the muscle (p. 10).
topics.mechanism: 1) A new movement starts as a conscious plan in the motor cortex. 2) Repetition fires the same neurons-muscles circuit again and again. 3) The connection strengthens and the sequence can be triggered with less cortical effort. 4) The movement becomes automatic, freeing conscious attention for other things.
components: Motor cortex: plans and initiates voluntary movement
Neural pathway: the strengthened circuit linking brain and muscles
Perimysium: connective tissue sheath around muscle fibre bundles (p. 10)
Fasciculus: bundles of fibres within muscle (p. 10)

examples.title: Learning to drive a manual car
examples.text: Clutch, gear and mirrors demand full attention at first; after months the same sequence runs itself while you hold a conversation. Repetition built the shortcut.
examples.mechanism: Strengthened motor circuits let the sequence run with minimal conscious control.

examples.title: A pianist's scales
examples.text: A musician plays scales while reading different music: the scale pattern is stored as a strong brain-muscle connection, released without deliberate thought.
examples.mechanism: Repeated firing made the motor sequence automatic.

examples.title: Toddlers falling while learning to walk
examples.text: A baby's early wobbles reflect unfinished pathways; months of practice wire the balance-walking circuit the book describes (p. 9).
examples.mechanism: Trial and error plus repetition form the walking pathways.

connections: Same strengthening principle as learning (c16) and brain plasticity (c09t3).

chapters.title: Unraveling the Nervous System
chapters.intro: Human beings are wonderfully complex: trillions of cells assembling into tissues, organs and bones, all coordinated by a control centre, the nervous system: the brain, spinal cord and reams of nerves (p. 12). This chapter maps its hierarchies, explains how feelings move the body, and tours the fight-or-flight response and major nervous disorders.
objectives: Describe the hierarchy of nerve structures
Split the nervous system into central and peripheral parts
Explain sympathetic vs parasympathetic responses
Recognise major nervous-system disorders covered on p. 18

topics.title: The nervous system and its hierarchies

intro.what: The body-wide control network: brain, spinal cord and peripheral nerves, organised in hierarchies.
intro.why: Without it, trillions of cells could not act as one organism.
intro.where: Brain and spinal cord centrally; nerves branching to every tissue peripherally.
intro.problem: Coordinating movement, sensation and organ function across the whole body.

topics.explanation: The book opens the chapter with scale: humans are gargantuan superstructures compared to single-celled organisms, boasting trillions of cells that assemble and maintain specialised tissues, organs and bones. This complexity is only possible because a coordination centre monitors and controls the actions of the whole body: the nervous system (p. 12). It asks you to learn the hierarchies of nerve structures that keep you alive (p. 13): the brain at the top, the spinal cord as the main trunk, and peripheral nerves branching outward to skin, muscles and organs. The system has two great divisions: the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (everything else), which further splits into the voluntary nerves that move your body and the autonomic nerves that run organs automatically. Your nervous system also rescues you: reflex responses pull your hand off a hot surface before conscious thought catches up (p. 14).
topics.mechanism: Sensory nerves report the body's state upward; the brain and spinal cord decide; motor nerves carry commands outward. Reflexes shortcut the decision: sensory input connects to spinal circuits that trigger motor output directly, which is why rescue happens faster than thought.
components: Central nervous system: brain + spinal cord
Peripheral nervous system: nerves outside brain and spinal cord
Voluntary (somatic) division: conscious movement
Autonomic division: automatic organ control
Reflex arc: spinal rescue circuit (p. 14)

takeaways: The nervous system is the coordination centre for trillions of cells (p. 12).
Its hierarchy: brain → spinal cord → peripheral nerves (p. 13).

topics.title: How feelings affect the body: relax or react

intro.what: The autonomic tug-of-war between the calming parasympathetic system and the mobilising sympathetic system.
intro.why: Explains why stress changes your heart rate, digestion and breathing.
intro.where: Autonomic nerves run to heart, lungs, gut, skin and eyes.
intro.problem: The body must switch between rest-and-digest and fight-or-flight as danger demands (pp. 15-17).

topics.explanation: How we feel can affect our body in many ways (p. 15). When we're free from periods of stress, our body responds by reverting to a more balanced state of rest and digest: the parasympathetic nervous system at work. When we feel threatened, the sympathetic nervous system takes over: heart rate climbs, breathing quickens, digestion pauses, and blood is directed to the muscles. The book frames the choice as 'a bear or a boss?' (p. 16): whether the threat is a predator or a deadline, the fight-or-flight response prepares the body the same way, an ancient survival program repurposed for modern stressors (p. 16). As the connective network coordinates these shifts, chronic activation matters: staying in fight-or-flight mode constantly stresses the cardiovascular and digestive systems (p. 17). The practical lesson: recovery periods are not laziness; they are the parasympathetic system doing maintenance.
topics.mechanism: Threat detected → amygdala and hypothalamus trigger sympathetic output → adrenal glands release adrenaline → heart and breathing rates rise, digestion slows, pupils widen. Threat passes → parasympathetic nerves reverse the changes, restoring rest and digest.
components: Sympathetic nervous system: mobilises the body for action
Parasympathetic nervous system: restores rest and digest (p. 15)
Adrenaline: chemical messenger of the fight-or-flight response
Amygdala/hypothalamus: brain trigger points for the switch

examples.title: Interview nerves
examples.text: Before an interview your heart pounds and your mouth is dry, even though no bear is present: the same ancient program fires for a boss as for a predator (p. 16).
examples.mechanism: Sympathetic activation triggered by perceived social threat.

examples.title: Afternoon crash after a stressful morning
examples.text: Once the stressor passes, parasympathetic activity dominates and drowsiness follows as the body rebalances.
examples.mechanism: Parasympathetic rebound restoring rest and digest.

examples.title: Watching a horror film

examples.mechanism: Brief sympathetic spikes followed by recovery.

topics.title: Reflexes and when the system breaks: neuropathy, Parkinson's and more

intro.what: The reflex arc in action, and a tour of nervous-system disorders the book lists on p. 18, including peripheral neuropathy and Parkinson's.
intro.why: Reflexes show the system's speed; disorders show what happens when parts of it fail.
intro.where: Reflex circuits in the spinal cord; disorders affect peripheral nerves or the brain.
intro.problem: Injury and disease disrupt signalling, producing numbness, tremor or lost control.

topics.explanation: Your nervous system rescues you from harm through reflexes (p. 14). The complete circuit is fast because it is short: a sensory neuron detects danger, a spinal relay passes the signal across, and a motor neuron fires the muscle. The brain is informed afterwards, which is why you act before you feel. On p. 18 the book surveys what happens when the network breaks: peripheral neuropathy, where damaged peripheral nerves cause numbness, tingling or pain, often starting in the feet and hands; Parkinson's, where dopamine-producing cells in the brain degenerate, producing tremor, stiffness and slowed movement; and other conditions affecting the connective network that coordinates the body (p. 17-18). These conditions matter because they show the system's design logic: damage in the cables (neuropathy) versus damage in the control room (Parkinson's) produce very different symptoms.
topics.mechanism: Reflex: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal interneuron → motor neuron → muscle, all within the spinal cord. Neuropathy: signal conduction in peripheral nerves degrades. Parkinson's: loss of dopamine signalling in motor circuits (the basal ganglia) disrupts smooth movement.

Peripheral nerves: vulnerable to neuropathy
Dopamine: messenger depleted in Parkinson's
Motor circuits: smoothness of movement depends on them

chapters.title: The Gut-Brain Axis
chapters.intro: Your gut and brain talk constantly. The book's section covers the gut-brain axis, and how probiotics and prebiotics may influence mood (pp. 20-21).
objectives: Describe the two-way communication between gut and brain
Explain the roles of the vagus nerve and gut microbes
Distinguish probiotics from prebiotics

topics.title: How your gut talks to your brain

intro.what: The gut-brain axis is the two-way communication network linking the digestive system and the brain.
intro.why: It explains why mood and digestion influence each other, and why what you eat can shape how you feel.
intro.where: The gut, its enteric nervous system, the vagus nerve, and the brain's mood circuits.
intro.problem: Mood and digestion are not separate systems: stress changes the gut, and the gut signals back to the brain.

topics.explanation: The gut contains its own extensive network of neurons, sometimes called the enteric nervous system or 'second brain', which manages digestion largely on its own while reporting upward. The main communication cable is the vagus nerve, a major highway running between the gut and the brain stem. Alongside the nerve signalling, trillions of gut microbes (the microbiome) digest food and produce chemical messengers that can influence mood and brain function. The book highlights this connection in a section on mood (p. 20), and specifically covers probiotics (live beneficial microbes) and prebiotics (the fibres that feed them), noting their potential role in supporting mood and gut health (p. 21). Evidence from research into mood and diet is still developing, so treat strong claims cautiously; but the two-way traffic itself is well established.
topics.mechanism: 1) Food and stress signals shape the gut environment. 2) Gut cells and microbes produce signalling chemicals. 3) The vagus nerve carries gut signals to the brain stem, and brain signals back down. 4) Brain mood circuits and gut function adjust each other in both directions.
components: Enteric nervous system: the gut's own nerve network
Vagus nerve: the main gut-brain highway
Microbiome: trillions of gut microbes
Probiotics: live beneficial microbes (p. 21)
Prebiotics: fibres that feed beneficial microbes (p. 21)

examples.mechanism: Brain-to-gut signalling via the autonomic and vagus routes.

chapters.title: The Science of Pain
chapters.intro: Pain is not just a sensation; it is the brain's alarm and protection system. The book dedicates a multi-page section to the science of pain: the pain pathway, types of pain, killing pain, chronic pain and treatment (pp. 21-27), including gate control theory explained through a stubbed toe.
objectives: Trace the pain pathway from injury to brain

topics.title: The pain pathway and types of pain

intro.what: The route pain signals take from injured tissue to conscious experience, and the categories pain falls into.
intro.why: Understanding the pathway explains why pain can be blocked at different points.
intro.where: From receptors in skin and tissue, up spinal tracts, to the brain's pain-processing regions.
intro.problem: Pain protects us, but it can malfunction and persist long after injury heals.

topics.explanation: Pain begins with specialised receptors called nociceptors, which respond to damaging mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli. Their signals travel along sensory neurons into the spinal cord, cross to the opposite side, and ascend to the brain, where regions including the thalamus and cortex make the signal conscious and locate it in the body. The book distinguishes types of pain (pp. 23-24): acute pain, the useful alarm of immediate injury; chronic pain, which persists beyond normal healing; and neuropathic pain, caused by damaged nerves themselves firing without injury. The section opens with the striking idea that pain is generated by the brain as an experience, not simply passively received: the same injury can hurt differently depending on context, attention and expectation. That is why distraction, fear and even mood change pain intensity (pp. 22-24).
topics.mechanism: Injury → nociceptors fire → signal ascends the spinal cord via dedicated tracts → thalamus relays → cortex interprets and localises → emotional regions assign urgency. Descending pathways from the brain can dial the signal up or down at the spinal relay, the biological basis of context-dependent pain.
components: Nociceptors: danger-detecting receptors
Spinal tracts: the ascending pain cables
Thalamus: relay station
Cortex: conscious, located pain
Descending modulation: brain-controlled volume knob

topics.title: Gate control theory, killing pain and chronic pain treatment

intro.what: Gate control theory, the spinal 'gate' that can shut pain out, plus how over-the-counter painkillers work and how chronic pain is treated.
intro.why: These are the book's practical answers to pain management (pp. 24-27).
intro.where: The spinal cord dorsal horn for the gate; body tissues and liver for painkiller action.
intro.problem: If pain were a simple wire, rubbing a bumped elbow could not help; the gate explains why it does.

topics.explanation: Gate control theory (pp. 25-26) proposes that a mechanism in the spinal cord acts like a gate: signals from large touch fibres, such as those activated by rubbing a bumped elbow, can inhibit the smaller pain fibres' signals before they ascend. The classic example the book uses is the stubbed toe: hopping and rubbing the toe floods the gate with touch input, reducing the pain that reaches the brain (p. 26). This is why rubbing, vibration and warmth can genuinely reduce pain. On killing pain (pp. 26-27), the book covers over-the-counter painkillers: paracetamol and NSAIDs like ibuprofen reduce pain by acting at the source of inflammation and on signalling, while stronger opioids act on receptors in the brain and spinal cord to damp the whole alarm system. For chronic pain treatment (p. 27), the emphasis is broader: because chronic pain involves sensitised pathways and psychology, treatment combines medication, physical rehabilitation, and psychological approaches rather than drugs alone.
topics.mechanism: Gate control: touch-fibre input activates inhibitory interneurons in the spinal dorsal horn, which suppress pain-fibre transmission upward. Painkillers: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-driven inflammation at the injury; paracetamol acts centrally; opioids bind receptors in brain and spinal cord, damping transmission.

Touch fibres: large fibres that can close the gate
OTC painkillers: paracetamol, ibuprofen (p. 27)
Chronic pain care: drugs + rehab + psychology (p. 27)

chapters.title: The Blood-Brain Barrier and the Pituitary Gland
chapters.intro: Two compact but critical sections close the biology block: what the blood-brain barrier is (p. 28) and the pituitary gland up close (p. 28).
objectives: Explain what the blood-brain barrier admits and blocks

topics.title: The blood-brain barrier

intro.what: A selective border of cells lining the brain's blood vessels that strictly controls what enters brain tissue.
intro.why: The brain needs stable chemistry and protection from toxins and pathogens.
intro.where: Capillaries throughout the brain.
intro.problem: Blood carries nutrients, but also wastes, toxins and immune cells that could harm neurons.

topics.explanation: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by tightly joined cells lining the brain's capillaries. Unlike vessels elsewhere in the body, which leak freely, brain capillaries admit only what the brain needs: oxygen, glucose and small lipid-soluble molecules, while blocking most large molecules, toxins and many drugs. This selectivity is why some medicines that work elsewhere in the body cannot reach the brain: drug designers must either use molecules that cross the barrier or deliver them directly. The barrier also protects the brain from infection, but at a cost: immune cells largely cannot enter, so brain infections are serious and hard to treat. The book positions the BBB within its anatomy tour of the brain's defences (p. 28).
topics.mechanism: Endothelial cells in brain capillaries are joined by tight junctions, sealing the gaps. Transport systems ferry permitted molecules across; everything else must be small and fat-soluble, or carried by a specific transporter, to enter.
components: Tight junctions: the seals between capillary cells
Transporters: gatekeepers for glucose and amino acids
Lipid solubility: the property that lets some drugs cross

examples.title: Why some cold medicines don't touch the brain

examples.mechanism: Lipid-soluble molecules pass the capillary seals.

topics.title: The pituitary gland up close

intro.what: A pea-sized gland under the brain that releases hormones controlling growth, metabolism, stress and reproduction.
intro.why: It is the hormonal command post translating brain signals into body-wide chemistry.
intro.where: Sits beneath the hypothalamus at the brain's base.
intro.problem: The brain runs on electricity; the body also needs chemical broadcasting, which is the pituitary's job.

topics.explanation: The pituitary gland (p. 28) hangs below the hypothalamus and works with it: the hypothalamus monitors the body's state and sends controlling signals to the pituitary, which releases hormones into the blood. These hormones direct other glands: the thyroid for metabolic rate, the adrenals for stress responses, and the reproductive glands. Growth hormone released by the pituitary drives childhood growth and tissue repair. The pituitary is often called the master gland because its outputs cascade across the body, though it ultimately takes orders from the hypothalamus, keeping the brain in charge. In this way the brain runs two parallel control systems: fast electrical signalling through nerves, and slower chemical signalling through hormones.
topics.mechanism: Hypothalamus detects need → releases releasing factors → pituitary secretes its hormone → target gland acts → feedback signals return to hypothalamus to adjust output.

Hypothalamus: its upstairs controller
Growth hormone: growth and repair
Adrenal/thyroid axes: downstream targets

chapters.title: How the Brain Sees
chapters.intro: Seeing happens in the brain, not the eye. This section covers how the brain sees (p. 30) and how images are formed within the eyes (pp. 29-32), closing with how animal eyes compare.
objectives: Trace light from object to visual cortex
Explain the retina's role and the optic chiasm crossing

topics.title: From light waves to the visual cortex

intro.what: The full visual pipeline: light, eye optics, retinal cells, optic nerves and cortical processing.
intro.why: Vision is the brain's dominant sense and a model for all sensory processing.
intro.where: From the outside world through the eyes to the occipital cortex at the brain's back.
intro.problem: The eyes do not produce images; they simply take in light waves and pass on information (p. 30).

topics.explanation: Light reflects off objects and enters the eye through the pupil, where it is refracted by the lens and cornea so rays reach the retina at the back of the eye (p. 29). The retina is a sensory membrane of millions of light-sensitive cells: rods for dim light, cones for colour and detail. When light waves hit the retina they activate certain cells, which fire electrical signals down the optic nerves. The nerves meet and cross at the optic chiasm, so signals from each eye's left visual field go to the brain's right side and vice versa (p. 30). No images are formed within the eyes themselves; the brain assembles the picture: visual areas in the occipital cortex process edges, motion, colour and form, and higher regions recognise objects and faces (c08). The section closes with how animal eyes differ, from colour ranges to night vision (pp. 31-32).
topics.mechanism: Light → cornea and lens focus → retina rods/cones convert to electrical signals → optic nerves → optic chiasm crossing → occipital visual cortex processes features → higher areas interpret meaning.

Retina: light-sensitive membrane of rods and cones (p. 29)
Optic nerve: cable to the brain

chapters.title: Never Forget a Face
chapters.intro: Why do some faces stick while others vanish? This section covers face recognition and its failure, prosopagnosia (pp. 32-33).
objectives: Describe how the brain specialises in face recognition
Explain prosopagnosia and what it reveals about processing

topics.title: Face recognition and prosopagnosia

intro.what: The brain's dedicated machinery for recognising faces, and the condition where it fails.
intro.why: Faces are the most socially important visual objects, so the brain dedicates special resources to them.
intro.where: A region on the underside of the temporal-occipital cortex, often called the fusiform face area.
intro.problem: Recognising a face is not the same as recognising any object; damage reveals the difference.

topics.explanation: We recognise thousands of faces across decades, often from brief or partial views. The brain handles faces with dedicated processing: the fusiform face area responds far more strongly to faces than to other objects. The book explains that we process faces holistically, reading the whole configuration of eyes, nose and mouth at once rather than as separate features, which is why a subtle change in eye spacing is instantly noticeable (pp. 32-33). The flip side is prosopagnosia, or face blindness: after damage to that region, or developmentally, a person sees a face perfectly well yet cannot tell whose it is, sometimes not even their own in a mirror. They may rely on voice, gait or clothing instead. The condition demonstrates that recognition is a separate brain function from seeing: the image arrives fine, the naming step fails.
topics.mechanism: Face image → visual cortex extracts features → fusiform face area matches the configuration against stored face representations → recognition and memory of the person activate. Damage to the matching step leaves vision intact but recognition absent.
components: Fusiform face area: face-specialised cortical region
Holistic processing: whole-configuration recognition
Prosopagnosia: face blindness from damage or development

chapters.title: The Science Behind Your Accent
chapters.intro: Why you speak the way you do: the science behind your accent (pp. 33-37), plus brain plasticity, how the brain rewires itself (pp. 35-36).

topics.title: Accents, speech circuits and critical periods

intro.what: How the brain builds an accent: learned sound patterns laid down early in speech circuits.
intro.why: Accents are a visible trace of brain development and language learning.
intro.where: Speech and hearing circuits across temporal and frontal areas.
intro.problem: Why do late learners keep their accent while children blend in seamlessly?

topics.explanation: An accent is a habit of sound production: which vowels you stretch, which consonants you drop, which rhythm you follow. These patterns are learned during childhood, when speech circuits are highly mouldable. The book explains that children exposed to a language early absorb its sound system almost perfectly, while adults learning later typically keep traces of their first language's sounds because their speech circuits have settled (pp. 33-35). This window is a critical period: after it, producing native-like sounds takes deliberate training and even then rarely reaches effortless nativeness. Accents also mark social identity, which is why they persist: they signal where you belong. Crucially, an accent is not a deficit; it is a record of your linguistic history written into your speech circuits.
topics.mechanism: Early exposure tunes auditory discrimination and motor programmes for that language's sounds. After the critical period, established motor programmes interfere with new ones, producing accented speech.

Critical period: early window of peak mouldability
Motor programmes: learned production patterns

topics.title: Brain plasticity: the rewiring brain

intro.what: Brain plasticity: the brain's lifelong ability to reorganise its connections through experience.
intro.why: It underpins recovery after injury, learning at any age, and habit change.
intro.where: Synapses throughout the cortex; affected regions reallocate resources.
intro.problem: The brain is not hard-wired: circuits adjust to what you practise and what you lose.

topics.explanation: The brain is plastic: its wiring changes with use (pp. 35-36). The principle is use it or lose it: practised connections strengthen; unused ones weaken. Studies of musicians show enlarged cortical areas for the fingers they exercise most; learning a second language reshapes auditory regions; after a stroke, neighbouring regions can partly take over lost functions through rehabilitation. Plasticity is strongest in childhood, which is why languages and instruments come easier early (see c09t1), but it never fully stops. What changes with age is effort: adult rewiring requires repetition and attention, while children absorb almost incidentally. Plasticity also has a caution: the same mechanism that builds skill consolidates bad habits and chronic stress patterns.
topics.mechanism: Repeated activation of a circuit → synapses in it strengthen → more resources and area are allocated → the skill becomes easier. Disuse → synapses weaken → capacity reallocates elsewhere.

chapters.title: Sleep: Why Do We Sleep?
chapters.intro: A third of your life happens asleep, and the brain is busy the whole time. This section covers why we sleep (p. 48) and the brain activity of sleep stages, including the thalamus and REM (pp. 47-49).
objectives: Explain the main theories of why we sleep

Connect sleep to memory consolidation

topics.title: Why we sleep and what the sleeping brain does

intro.what: The functions of sleep: restoration, memory consolidation and processing, organised in repeating stages.
intro.why: Sleep shapes learning, mood and health, so understanding it changes daily decisions.
intro.where: Whole-brain activity cycling through stages, involving the thalamus and cortex.
intro.problem: Why spend a third of life unconscious? Sleep is active maintenance, not shutdown.

topics.explanation: Why do we sleep? (p. 48) The leading answers: restoration, the brain repairs itself and clears metabolic waste; memory consolidation, the day's experiences are replayed and filed into long-term storage; and protection, conserving energy and keeping us safe in the dangerous dark. Sleep proceeds in cycles: light sleep, deep slow-wave sleep where the brain synchronises and the body repairs, then REM (rapid eye movement) sleep, when the brain is nearly as active as waking, dreams are vivid, and the body's muscles are switched off to prevent acting dreams out. During REM the thalamus, which normally gates sensory information into the cortex, changes behaviour so that internally generated dream images take the cortical stage (p. 49). Skipping sleep damages exactly these processes: memory suffers, mood destabilises, and attention collapses. The practical science: the deepest consolidation happens in the night's later REM-rich cycles, which is why a full night beats a truncated one.

chapters.title: Nightmares, Phobias and Everyday Fears
chapters.intro: Fear is ancient machinery running in modern life. This section explains nightmares, phobias and everyday fears (pp. 50-56), from why we dream badly to why spiders and snakes unsettle us innately.

topics.explanation: Nightmares happen mainly in REM sleep, when the emotional brain, led by the amygdala, is highly active while the reasoning prefrontal cortex is dialed down. One view the book supports: dreaming lets the brain rehearse threats safely, a kind of night-time simulator running fear scenarios without real stakes (pp. 50-51). Bad dreams cluster around waking stress, and repeated nightmares can follow trauma. Occasionally dreamers become aware they are dreaming, lucid dreaming, which researchers study as a window into consciousness. Most nightmares are normal and occasional; they become a problem when they recur nightly and disrupt sleep, which is the point to seek help.

topics.explanation: A phobia is more than dislike: it is a fear response out of proportion to real danger, persisting and triggering avoidance (pp. 52-56). The book highlights our innate unease around spiders and snakes as a survival tactic that warned us of potential dangers (p. 56): our ancestors who feared the right things survived. But not every fear is innate: phobias are learned through bad experiences, witnessed panic or cultural messaging, then stored as strong emotional memories. The section also tours specific fear domains covered in the book, from fear of animals (the snake-fangs discussion, p. 53) to unusual modern fears, and everyday fears such as public speaking. The striking asymmetry: we can learn to fear the ancient dangers in a single trial, while modern hazards are statistically deadlier yet feel calmer. Treatment works by gradually retraining the fear system: controlled, repeated safe exposure lets the amygdala update its alarm list.

chapters.title: The Science of Emotions
chapters.intro: What is an emotion, physically? The psychology part opens with the science of emotions (pp. 59-65): brain regions, survival tactics, and how feelings shape the body.

topics.title: What emotions are and where they live

intro.what: Emotions: coordinated brain-and-body states that prepare action and signal value.
intro.why: Emotions drive decisions, memory and health; they are not noise on top of thinking.
intro.where: Amygdala, hypothalamus, insula and cortex, wired to the body through the autonomic system.
intro.problem: How does a chemical-and-circuit event become a feeling?

topics.explanation: An emotion is the brain's rapid appraisal of a situation plus the body's preparation to act on it. The book walks through how we feel can affect our body in many ways (p. 59-60): fear raises heart rate, joy relaxes, stress tenses muscles and disturbs digestion. Brain imaging links specific feelings to specific structures: the amygdala lights up for fear and threat, the insula for disgust, reward circuits for pleasure and joy. Emotions evolved as survival tactics (p. 64): fear warned of predators, disgust warned of spoiled food and contagion, anger mobilised defence. They also coordinate socially: expressions broadcast our states to others, letting groups cooperate. Modern life repurposes this old machinery: a tense meeting triggers the same circuits a predator once did, which is why feelings feel disproportionate at times.
topics.mechanism: Stimulus → rapid appraisal (amygdala fast path; cortex slower, more accurate path) → body response via autonomic and hormonal systems → feedback from the body shapes the conscious feeling.

chapters.title: Why Do We Lie?
chapters.intro: Lying is not unique to humans (p. 66). This section covers why we lie, when lying develops, and what body language reveals (pp. 65-70).

topics.title: The lying brain and body language

intro.what: The cognitive machinery of deception and the physical traces it may leave.
intro.why: Lying requires theory of mind, planning and control, so it is a window into social cognition.

topics.explanation: Lying is not unique to humans (p. 66): other animals use deception, from birds feigning injury to distract predators to primates hiding food. In children, classic developmental work found that lying emerges alongside social understanding: the youngest children cannot yet deceive; by the preschool years most can pass a simple false-belief task and tell a deliberate lie (p. 67). Lying is cognitively expensive: the deceiver must hold the truth in mind, construct the false version, monitor the listener, and suppress leaks, which is why the prefrontal cortex carries the load. On body language (pp. 68-70): the popular signs, gaze aversion, fidgeting, are unreliable single cues. Stress marks can indicate discomfort without guilt. The strongest sign of deception is a mismatch in detail: inconsistent accounts, not shifting eyes. The book's stance is sceptical of lie-detection folklore and supportive of evidence-based reading.
topics.mechanism: Deciding to lie → prefrontal planning constructs the falsehood → inhibitory control suppresses truthful responses → stress response may leak via autonomic signs → the listener reads imperfect cues.

topics.title: Hypnosis: trance, suggestion and real effects

intro.what: Hypnosis: a state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility, used clinically for pain and habit change.
intro.why: It tests the boundary between mind and brain: suggestion measurably changes perception and pain.
intro.where: Altered activity across attention and control networks.
intro.problem: Is it theatre, placebo, or a real shift in brain state? Evidence says it is a real, if variable, phenomenon.

topics.explanation: Hypnosis is not sleep and not mind control: it is deep focused attention with heightened responsiveness to suggestion (p. 70). Brain-imaging studies show real changes in activity and connectivity under suggestion, and the effects are measurable: hypnotic suggestion can reduce the perceived intensity of pain (pp. 71-72). The book highlights cases of surgery carried out under hypnosis with reduced anaesthetic needs (p. 72), which remains rare and requires exceptionally responsive subjects, but demonstrates the effect is not mere compliance. Crucially, people differ: a minority are highly hypnotisable, most are moderately so, and a minority barely at all, which is why stage 'hypnotised' volunteers are drawn from volunteers who respond strongly. Hypnosis in animals (p. 73) covers tonic immobility-like responses such as 'animal hypnosis', an innate stillness response rather than the human phenomenon. Clinical uses include pain management, anxiety and habit change; it is not a magic erase for memory or a cure-all.

chapters.intro: The book counts about 86 billion neurons in the human brain and asks how learning physically happens: neurons, astrocytes, sea slugs and long-term potentiation (pp. 73-78).

topics.title: Neurons, astrocytes and how learning happens

intro.what: The cellular basis of learning: strengthening connections between neurons, with astrocytes as support cells.

topics.explanation: The brain holds roughly 86 billion neurons, each connecting to thousands of others (p. 74). Learning is not adding neurons; it is tuning connections: repeatedly used synapses strengthen, a phenomenon called long-term potentiation (LTP). The book tells the story of Eric Kandel's experiments on the sea slug Aplysia (p. 76): a simple animal with large, accessible neurons, where repeated stimulation produced lasting changes in the strength of connections, revealing the cellular mechanism of memory and earning a Nobel Prize. Alongside neurons, the book introduces astrocytes (p. 76), star-shaped support cells once dismissed as packing material, now known to regulate synapses, supply nutrients and participate in signalling, increasingly implicated in learning. Habituation and sensitisation, the slug's decreasing or increasing responses to stimuli, map neatly to human learning: repeated exposure without consequence dulls response; meaningful, salient events stick.
topics.mechanism: Repeated co-activation of neurons → synapses strengthen (LTP) via signalling changes → the circuit representing the skill or fact becomes faster and more reliable → consolidation during sleep stabilises it.

chapters.title: Human, Machine and Evolutionary Learning

topics.title: Three learners: brains, machines, evolution

intro.what: A comparison of three learning systems: neural learning in individuals, machine learning in computers, and evolutionary learning across generations.

intro.problem: Each system adapts, but on very different timescales and with different materials.

topics.explanation: A brain learns within a lifetime, tuning synapses from experience in seconds to years. A machine learning system learns by adjusting model parameters from data, often needing thousands to millions of examples where a child needs a handful, but able to process far more data than any person. Evolution learns across generations: genes that produce better survival are selected, a process exquisitely slow but unimaginably parallel, running on every reproducing organism simultaneously (pp. 78-79). The comparison shows trade-offs: brains are data-efficient but biased by experience; machines are data-hungry but tireless; evolution is slow but world-changing. Human learning sits uniquely between: we inherit a tuned brain from evolution, then rapidly adapt it to our specific world in childhood.

chapters.title: How Optical Illusions Work
chapters.intro: Your brain edits everything you see. This section explains how optical illusions work (pp. 79-84), including colour correction and the Ames room.

topics.title: Illusions: the brain's editing software exposed

intro.what: Optical illusions: images that trigger predictable errors in the brain's visual interpretation.
intro.why: Illusions are the debug mode of vision, exposing the shortcuts the brain normally uses invisibly.
intro.where: Visual cortex and higher interpretation areas.
intro.problem: Vision is construction, not a camera; illusions prove it.

topics.explanation: The brain does not passively record the world; it constructs a useful model, and illusions catch the construction machinery in the act (pp. 79-84). Three illustrations: first, colour correction, or colour constancy: the brain compensates for lighting, which is why a white shirt looks white at sunset, and why the same colour swatch can look dramatically different against two backgrounds; the famous brain-tweaking dress debate hinged on exactly this. Second, geometric illusions: lines that look bent or lengths that look unequal because context and depth cues bias the interpretation, even when you can measure they are identical. Third, the Ames room: a deliberately distorted room that, viewed through a fixed peephole, makes a person walking across it appear to grow or shrink, because the brain insists on assuming rooms are rectangular and therefore explains away the room's distortion by changing the person's size instead (pp. 83-84). The lesson: perception is prediction, and illusions are its failures made visible.
topics.mechanism: The brain applies assumptions (uniform lighting, rectangular rooms, depth from context) to raw retinal input. When an image violates the assumption in a crafted way, the output is a systematic, repeatable error.

topics.title: Puzzles, pressure and collaboration

intro.what: Escape rooms: timed puzzle environments that exercise perception, memory, logic and teamwork.

intro.problem: Why do some teams solve puzzles that stump clever individuals?

topics.explanation: An escape room is a controlled problem environment: a time limit, layered puzzles and a team (pp. 85-88). Three lessons emerge. First, perspective: individuals get stuck in ruts, fixating on one interpretation of a clue, and a teammate's fresh eyes break the fixation, which is why mixed teams outperform solo solvers. Second, pressure: the countdown sharpens focus for some and floods working memory for others, showing stress's inverted-U effect on performance. Third, communication: teams that externalise their thinking, saying aloud what they see and trying patterns, solve faster than silent teams, because speech organises working memory and distributes the load. The book ties this to everyday problem-solving: the same mechanics govern exams, workplace projects and any deadline.
topics.mechanism: Novel puzzle → attention and working memory load increase → fixation on one interpretation blocks alternatives → fresh perspectives or verbalising disrupt the fixation → solution insight follows re-encoding of the problem.

topics.title: Intelligence, IQ and what they measure

intro.what: Intelligence as measurable cognitive ability: what IQ tests capture, and the fluid/crystallised distinction.
intro.why: Knowing what IQ does and does not measure prevents both over-rating and dismissing it.
intro.where: Networks across the cortex; performance depends on the whole brain's efficiency.
intro.problem: Is intelligence fixed? What do the regions of the brain contribute? (p. 92)

topics.explanation: The book asks what roles the different regions of our brains play in our intellect, with an 'inside the brain' map of contributions such as the frontal lobe's role in reasoning and planning (p. 92). Intelligence research distinguishes fluid intelligence, the raw processing power for novel problems, and crystallised intelligence, the accumulated knowledge and skills of a lifetime. The book relays the developmental evidence: crystalline intelligence more or less grows all life long, whereas fluid intelligence grows up to around the 20s, then flattens and later declines (p. 96). An IQ score summarises performance on standardised reasoning tasks; it predicts some real-world outcomes on average, but is a snapshot of test performance, not a ceiling, and says nothing about creativity, drive or specific talents. Sleep, exercise and practice measurably move day-to-day cognitive performance, which is the practical point of the book's closing tips (pp. 93-95): treat the brain like an athlete treats the body.
topics.mechanism: Test performance reflects processing speed, working memory capacity and knowledge access. Fluid tasks load working memory and novelty; crystallised tasks load stored knowledge.
components: Fluid intelligence: novel-problem processing power
Crystallised intelligence: accumulated knowledge (p. 96)
IQ: a standardised summary score, not a destiny
Frontal lobe: planning and reasoning contributions (p. 92)

topics.title: Brain training and ten ways to think smarter

intro.what: The brain-training evidence and the book's ten practical tips, with expert commentary from the University of Sheffield explaining that brain training might not be for everyone.
intro.why: Separates the hype from what actually works.
intro.where: Whole-brain habits: sleep, exercise, diet, learning and social engagement.
intro.problem: Do puzzle apps make you smarter? Mostly no; lifestyle and real learning do more.

topics.explanation: A neuroscientist at the University of Sheffield explains some of the evidence behind brain training and how it might not be for everyone (pp. 95-96): practising a task makes you better at that task, but the gains rarely transfer broadly to general intelligence. The developmental evidence also shows the age effect: both fluid and crystallised measures grow through life but follow different curves (p. 96). The book's own list of tips (pp. 93-95) is more grounded: sleep well, since consolidation and attention both depend on it; exercise, which supports blood flow and mood; keep learning genuinely new things, which is real training for real circuits; stay socially engaged; manage stress; and feed the brain adequately. The honest summary: there is no shortcut; the boring fundamentals, sleep, exercise, learning, stress control, outperform puzzle apps.
topics.mechanism: Task practice yields near transfer only. Lifestyle factors act on the brain's substrate: sleep consolidates, exercise supports vasculature and mood, novel learning drives plasticity (see c09t2, c16).
components: Near vs far transfer: the brain-training crux
Sleep, exercise, diet: the fundamentals
Novel learning: real circuit training
Stress management: protecting the machinery

examples.mechanism: Near transfer without far transfer.

brainRegions.name: Frontal lobe
brainRegions.location: Front of the brain, behind the forehead.
brainRegions.anatomy: The largest lobe, from the motor cortex strip back to the prefrontal regions.
brainRegions.function: Planning, reasoning, decision-making, voluntary movement, personality and speech production (Broca's area on the left).

brainRegions.name: Parietal lobe
brainRegions.anatomy: Between the frontal and occipital lobes, containing the somatosensory strip.
brainRegions.function: Touch, pressure, temperature and body-position sensing; spatial attention; integrating senses.

brainRegions.name: Temporal lobe
brainRegions.location: Sides of the brain, near the temples.
brainRegions.anatomy: Contains auditory cortex, language comprehension areas and the hippocampus inside.
brainRegions.function: Hearing, language comprehension, face recognition support, and memory formation via the hippocampus.

brainRegions.name: Occipital lobe
brainRegions.anatomy: Contains the primary visual cortex receiving the crossed optic signals.
brainRegions.function: Visual processing: edges, motion, colour and form, then object recognition.

brainRegions.name: Cerebellum
brainRegions.location: Lower back of the brain, under the occipital lobe.
brainRegions.anatomy: A densely folded structure holding most of the brain's neurons in a small volume.
brainRegions.function: Coordination, balance, timing and fine-tuning of movement; motor learning.

brainRegions.name: Brainstem
brainRegions.location: Base of the brain, continuing into the spinal cord.
brainRegions.anatomy: Midbrain, pons and medulla in one stalk.
brainRegions.function: Life support: breathing, heart rate, swallowing, sleep-wake switching, and the relay between body and cortex.

brainRegions.name: Thalamus
brainRegions.anatomy: A paired egg-shaped relay of nuclei.
brainRegions.function: Sensory and motor relay station; changes its gating during REM sleep (p. 49).

brainRegions.name: Hypothalamus
brainRegions.location: Below the thalamus, above the pituitary.
brainRegions.anatomy: A tiny cluster of nuclei with big influence.
brainRegions.function: Hunger, thirst, temperature, circadian timing, and control of the pituitary's hormones (p. 28).

brainRegions.name: Hippocampus
brainRegions.location: Inside the temporal lobe, one on each side.
brainRegions.anatomy: A curved structure shaped like a seahorse.
brainRegions.function: Forming new long-term memories and spatial navigation.
disorders: Amnesia when damaged (as in famous patient H.M.)

brainRegions.name: Amygdala
brainRegions.location: Deep in the temporal lobe, next to the hippocampus.
brainRegions.function: Fear learning and emotional memory; threat appraisal; active during nightmares and REM emotion (pp. 50-56).
disorders: Phobias and anxiety involve its alarm circuits (c12)

brainRegions.name: Basal ganglia
brainRegions.location: Deep on either side of the thalamus.
brainRegions.anatomy: A set of nuclei including the striatum and substantia nigra.
brainRegions.function: Movement control, habit formation and reward learning; dopamine circuits.

brainRegions.name: Cerebral cortex
brainRegions.anatomy: Roughly 2-4 mm of gray matter, folded into ridges and grooves.
brainRegions.function: Thoughts, memories, language, perception and conscious processing; gray matter outside, white matter inside (p. 8).
disorders: Lesions produce specific losses depending on location

sims.title: Neuron & Action Potential
sims.desc: Fire a neuron: watch the electrical signal race down the fibre, cross the synapse and trigger the next cell.
steps: Resting state: the neuron sits charged, waiting.
Input: signals arrive at the receiving branches.
Threshold: if inputs add up past the trigger point...
Fire! An electrical spike races down the axon.
Chemical hand-off: messengers cross the synapse to the next neuron.
Reset: the neuron recharges, ready to fire again.

sims.title: Reflex Arc
sims.desc: Touch the hot pan. Follow the signal from fingertip to spinal cord to muscle, faster than thought.
steps: Receptor: heat sensors in the skin fire.
Sensory neuron: the signal runs to the spinal cord.
Relay: inside the cord, the signal crosses to a motor neuron.
Motor command: 'withdraw!' races to the arm muscles.
Brain informed later: you consciously feel pain after your hand is already moving.

sims.title: Gate Control of Pain
sims.desc: The stubbed toe simulator. Compare pain with and without the rubbing that closes the spinal gate.
steps: Injury: pain fibres fire their alarm.
Gate: at the spinal relay, touch input competes with pain input.
Rub it: touch fibres flood the gate, inhibiting the pain signal.
Result: less pain reaches the brain; the same injury, a different experience.

sims.title: Fight or Flight
sims.desc: A bear (or a boss) appears. Flip between sympathetic and parasympathetic states and watch the body change.
steps: Threat detected: the amygdala sounds the alarm.
Sympathetic ON: heart races, breathing quickens, digestion pauses, pupils widen.
Threat passes: parasympathetic takes over.
Rest and digest: heart slows, digestion resumes, balance restored.

sims.title: Sleep Cycle
sims.desc: One night, compressed: watch the brain cycle through light, deep and REM stages and see what each does.
steps: Falling asleep: light sleep begins.
Deep sleep: slow waves, body repair, memory replay.
REM: brain near-waking, vivid dreams, muscles switched off.
Cycles repeat: deep sleep dominates early, REM grows toward morning.
Wake: refreshed circuits, consolidated memories.

sims.title: Fear Response & Phobia
sims.desc: See how the amygdala triggers the fear cascade, and how repeated safe exposure retrains the alarm.
steps: Cue spotted: the amygdala checks for threat.
Alarm: fear cascade fires before rational evaluation.
Safe repetition: controlled exposure creates new safe memories.
Retrained alarm: the response gradually quiets.

sims.title: From Light to Sight
sims.desc: Follow light waves into the eye, onto the retina, across the optic chiasm and into the visual cortex.
steps: Light enters through the pupil.
Cornea and lens focus the rays.
Retina: rods and cones convert light to signals.
Optic nerves cross at the chiasm.
Visual cortex assembles the image the eyes never formed.

sims.title: Neural Plasticity
sims.desc: Practise a skill in the sim and watch its circuit strengthen; stop practising and watch it fade.
steps: First try: a weak, wandering circuit.
Repetition: the same neurons fire together again and again.
Strengthening: synapses tune, the circuit sharpens.
Automatic: the skill runs itself, a neural shortcut.
Disuse: stop practising and the circuit slowly fades.
